title: When Your Inner Life and Outer Life Begin to Match
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer presents Step Three of her Leadership Connection Model -- Alignment of Purpose -- which asks leaders to examine whether their physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual lives are coherent with their stated values. She argues that misalignment is not merely uncomfortable but actively draining: the energy required to 'say one thing and live another' depletes leaders over time, and much of what we call burnout is actually prolonged disconnection from truth. Alignment is not perfection but the practice of incrementally closing the gap between what we know and how we live -- integrity in motion. When inner and outer lives begin to agree, leaders become steadier, more trustworthy, and more capable of creating impact that lasts. She closes with three reflection questions and a Lao Tzu quotation to ground the invitation practically.
points: * Misalignment -- having an inner life at odds with outer choices -- is exhausting and is often the real cause of what we label burnout. * Alignment of Purpose is not a luxury to postpone until 'the real work is done' -- it is the real work. * Integrity is alignment in motion: the active, daily practice of walking one's talk and closing the gap between knowing and living. * Expansion and growth are only sustainable when inner and outer lives are coherent enough to support the added weight of new responsibility. * Alignment rarely arrives all at once -- it begins with one honest act: a conversation, a boundary, a change in rhythm.
quotes: There is a point in every leadership journey when insight is no longer enough.
Not a complex question, but a profound one: Are you aligned physically, mentally, emotionally, and spiritually?
Misalignment is exhausting. It takes enormous energy to say one thing and live another.
Much of what we call burnout is prolonged disconnection from truth.
Alignment is integrity in motion, it is not perfection. It is the practice of walking your talk.
If we want change that lasts, we must live in a way that can hold it.
He who knows others is wise; he who knows himself is enlightened. -- Lao Tzu
